clinicalPearls: AApoAIV is a rare amyloidosis in which wild-type apolipoprotein A-IV deposits, resembling wild-type ATTR in being an acquired, age-related process rather than a classic hereditary disease.
It predominantly affects the kidney, characteristically the renal medulla, and the heart.
Renal disease presents as slowly progressive chronic kidney disease, often with only modest proteinuria.
It tends to occur in older individuals, consistent with an age-associated deposition of the normal-sequence protein.
There is usually no family history and no causative point mutation, which distinguishes it from the hereditary apolipoprotein amyloidoses.
Diagnosis requires biopsy with amyloid typing by mass spectrometry, as it is not detected by routine immunohistochemical panels and is easily missed.
There is no specific therapy; management is supportive with attention to renal and cardiac function.
reference.pathophysiology: Apolipoprotein A-IV is a plasma apolipoprotein involved in lipid transport and satiety signalling, secreted mainly by the intestine. In AApoAIV the wild-type protein deposits as amyloid, with a distinctive predilection for the renal medullary interstitium and, in some cases, the myocardium. The absence of a destabilising mutation and the older age of affected patients suggest an age-related acquired process analogous to wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis. Medullary deposition can impair urinary concentrating ability and contribute to slowly progressive renal dysfunction, while proteinuria is often modest because glomerular involvement is limited.
additionalDifferentials: Wild-type and variant ATTR for cardiac disease
Other infiltrative cardiomyopathies for cardiac-predominant cases
additionalInvestigations: Renal or cardiac biopsy with Congo red staining
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry, which is essential for identification
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
Echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers if cardiac involvement is suspected
SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden
Exclusion of ATTR by bone scintigraphy and TTR sequencing where relevant
redFlags: Slowly progressive renal impairment with a medullary pattern in an older patient
Amyloid that fails to type as AL, AA or ATTR on initial workup
reference.prognosis: AApoAIV is typically indolent and age-related, with slowly progressive renal and occasionally cardiac dysfunction. There is no disease-specific treatment, and the prognosis is generally more favourable than that of untreated AL amyloidosis.
pitfalls: Failing to identify the amyloid type because standard immunohistochemistry does not detect it
Misattributing renal decline to age or hypertension
Confusing cardiac AApoAIV with ATTR without confirmatory typing
Assuming a hereditary cause and pursuing unnecessary genetic testing of family members
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology, chapter on renal amyloidosis
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, chapter on amyloidosis
International Society of Amyloidosis nomenclature guidelines
management: Recognise there is no disease-specific or fibril-directed therapy, so management is supportive and organ-directed
Provide conservative chronic kidney disease care with renin-angiotensin blockade for proteinuria, blood-pressure control and treatment of anaemia and mineral-bone complications
Address the medullary concentrating defect with attention to hydration and electrolyte balance
Undertake cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers and treat any myocardial involvement with heart-failure therapy
Monitor renal function trajectory and plan renal replacement therapy or transplantation as chronic kidney disease advances
Refer to a specialist amyloidosis service and confirm the diagnosis by mass-spectrometry typing to avoid inappropriate treatment as AL amyloidosis
